title: The Long Road to Yorktown
protagonist: Sam Holt, a stable boy and message runner from Boston

passages.text: Your name is Sam Holt. You are fifteen. You sleep in the stable behind the Green Dragon Tavern in Boston. You feed the horses and run messages for men who whisper. It is April 18, 1775. A silversmith named Paul Revere comes through the back door fast. His boots are wet. He needs a horse, and he needs eyes on the road to Lexington. The British soldiers are moving tonight.

choices.text: Saddle his horse and ask to ride with him
Stay quiet and just hold the lantern

passages.text: You lead the fast brown mare into the yard. Across the dark water, two lanterns burn in the steeple of the Old North Church. Revere sees them too. "Two lights," he says. "The Regulars come by sea, across the Charles River." He pulls himself into the saddle. He looks down at you, breathing hard, and tells you the warning you must carry to every farmhouse before dawn.

question.question: What did the two lanterns in the Old North Church steeple signal on the night of Paul Revere's ride?
choices: The British troops were coming by water, across the Charles River
The British had already captured Boston harbor
The militia should surrender at Lexington
George Washington had arrived to take command
question.explanation: The signal was 'one if by land, two if by sea' — two lanterns meant the British Regulars were crossing the Charles River by boat.

choices.text: Ride hard toward Lexington with him
Wake the families on the near road first

passages.text: You gallop the dark roads. Dogs bark. Candles light up in windows. Revere shouts at every door, "The Regulars are out!" Riders join you, then split off to warn more towns. Near dawn a British patrol stops Revere on the road. They take his horse. But the warning is already ahead of him, racing house to house. You slip into the trees and keep moving toward Lexington Green.

choices.text: Go to the Green where the militia is forming
Push on to Concord to warn the powder stores

passages.text: Gray light. On Lexington Green about seventy farmers stand in a ragged line with muskets. Captain John Parker tells his men, "Stand your ground. Don't fire unless fired upon." The British column appears, hundreds of red coats, bayonets fixed. An officer screams for the farmers to throw down their arms. Then a shot cracks. No one knows who fired it. The British volley tears into the line. Eight men fall dead in the wet grass. You drop flat behind a stone wall, ears ringing.

choices.text: Run for Concord to warn them what's coming
Help drag a wounded farmer to cover

passages.text: By midmorning the fight reaches Concord. The British search for hidden gunpowder and cannon, but the colonists moved most of it days ago. Smoke rises from the town. At the North Bridge, militia from many towns gather on the far bank, hundreds of them now. They see the smoke and think Concord is burning. A British volley. The militia fire back. Redcoats fall. The famous shot is fired here, the one men will call the shot heard round the world. The British begin to retreat.

choices.text: Follow the retreat and carry word back to Boston
Stay and help the wounded on both sides

passages.text: The road back to Boston becomes a killing line. Militiamen crouch behind stone walls, trees, and barns. They fire at the red column the whole sixteen miles. British soldiers drop in the dust. Some colonists are shot in their own doorways. By night the British are back in Boston, bloodied. You sit in the stable, hands shaking. The war is real now. It will not stop.

choices.text: Join the militia camp surrounding Boston
Go home and try to stay out of it

passages.text: Thousands of New England militia ring Boston. They have courage but no order, no real general. In July 1775 a tall Virginian rides into the camp at Cambridge. The men say his name is George Washington, sent by the Continental Congress to command this Continental Army. He looks at the messy camp, the sick men, the empty powder casks, and his face goes hard. You are handed to his staff as a runner.

question.question: Why was George Washington chosen to command the Continental Army in 1775?
choices: Congress appointed him to lead and unify the colonial forces into one army
He had already defeated the British at Lexington
He was the king's cousin and demanded the post
He won an election held by the militia soldiers
question.explanation: The Continental Congress chose Washington to lead and organize the scattered militia into one unified Continental Army.

choices.text: Work hard to prove yourself to the general
Keep your head down and just carry mail

passages.text: Washington forces the British out of Boston in March 1776. Then he marches the army toward New York. In the summer you carry a packet south to Philadelphia, to the Continental Congress meeting in the State House. The streets buzz. Men argue about a word everyone is now saying out loud: independence. A thin, red-haired delegate from Virginia is writing something upstairs that will change everything.

choices.text: Deliver the packet to the State House yourself
Wait outside with the crowd

passages.text: Inside, the air is hot and still. The red-haired delegate is Thomas Jefferson. Papers cover his table. He looks up as you set down the packet. "We are not asking the king to fix things anymore," he says quietly. "We are telling the world we are free." On July 4, 1776, the Congress adopts his Declaration of Independence. You hear it read aloud in the square: that all men are created equal, with rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The crowd roars. Some weep. A king's statue is pulled down.

question.question: What did Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence, adopted July 4, 1776, mainly do?
choices: It declared the colonies free and independent and stated all men are created equal with rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
It asked King George III for a peace treaty and lower taxes
It made George Washington the king of America
It ended the war and freed all enslaved people immediately
question.explanation: Jefferson's Declaration announced independence and set out the idea that all men are created equal with unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

choices.text: Carry the news north to Washington's army
Sign up to serve directly with the army

passages.text: You reach Washington's army near New York with the Declaration in your pack. Then the British come. Their fleet fills the harbor. General Howe lands an army bigger than any city in America. At the Battle of Long Island the army is nearly crushed. Washington pulls his men across the East River at night in fog and boats, every man silent. Through the fall the British chase the army across New Jersey. Men desert. Winter comes. The cause is dying.

choices.text: Stay with the shrinking army through the retreat
Think hard about walking away home

passages.text: December 25, 1776. The army is starving and ragged on the Pennsylvania side of the Delaware River. Ice chokes the water. Washington gathers the men in the freezing dark. The password is Victory or Death. You climb into a long boat with soldiers whose feet are wrapped in rags. Some leave blood in the snow. Washington stands at the front of his boat, jaw set, as you cross the black, ice-filled river toward Trenton.

question.question: What bold move did Washington make on the night of December 25, 1776?
choices: He crossed the ice-filled Delaware River to surprise the enemy at Trenton
He surrendered his army to the British at Trenton
He sailed his whole army back to Boston
He retreated south to Virginia for the winter
question.explanation: Washington crossed the frozen Delaware on Christmas night and surprised the Hessian troops at Trenton, winning a desperately needed victory.

choices.text: Fight beside the men in the streets of Trenton
Run messages between Washington's columns

passages.text: At dawn you hit Trenton in a snowstorm. The Hessian soldiers, hired Germans fighting for the British, are caught half asleep. Cannon roar down the streets. The fight is short and brutal. Hundreds of Hessians surrender. The army wins. It is small, but it is a win, the first real one in months. Men who were ready to quit lift their heads again. The cause does not die this winter.

choices.text: Stay with the army into the next hard winter
Hope the worst is over now

passages.text: It is not over. The winter of 1777 and 1778 is worse. The army camps at Valley Forge in Pennsylvania. There are no warm clothes, little food, no shoes. You build huts from logs in the frozen mud. Smallpox and fever sweep the camp. Around two thousand men die that winter, not from bullets, but from cold and sickness and hunger. You bury friends in shallow, frozen graves. Each night you wonder if you will wake.

choices.text: Stay and drill with the dying army
Lie still and just try to survive the cold

passages.text: A loud Prussian officer named Baron von Steuben arrives. He cannot speak much English. He curses in German and French and makes his translator curse for him. But he teaches the ragged men to march, to load fast, to fight as one body. You drill until your hands bleed in the cold. By spring the starved survivors of Valley Forge are a real army. You are harder now, and proud of it.

choices.text: March out with the new, disciplined army

passages.text: You keep to your hut and your blanket. You do the smallest work you can. You watch men drill in the snow and feel nothing but cold. You trade your boots for bread. When spring comes, you are still alive, but thinner, quieter, emptied out. You have learned to feel nothing so the dying around you cannot reach you.

choices.text: March out with the army anyway

passages.text: Years pass. The war grinds on, north and south. France joins the American side and sends ships, money, and soldiers. A young French nobleman named the Marquis de Lafayette becomes one of Washington's most trusted generals, and he likes you, the runner who never quits. By 1781 the British general Cornwallis has marched his army to a small Virginia town on the water. Its name is Yorktown.

choices.text: Ride south with Washington's army toward Yorktown
Stay back with the supply trains

passages.text: The trap closes. Washington marches the American and French armies fast from the north. The French fleet under Admiral de Grasse beats the British navy at sea and seals the bay. Now Cornwallis cannot escape by water. Cannons are dragged into place. Trenches are dug closer and closer to the British lines. Lafayette finds you in the dust and grips your shoulder. "Tonight," he says, "we take their guns."

question.question: How did the French help trap Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781?
choices: The French fleet blocked the bay so the British army could not escape or be rescued by sea
The French king personally led the final charge
France convinced the British to surrender without a fight
The French burned Yorktown to the ground before the siege
question.explanation: The French navy under Admiral de Grasse controlled the Chesapeake Bay, cutting off Cornwallis's escape and sealing the British defeat at Yorktown.

choices.text: Volunteer for the night assault on the redoubts
Run powder and orders behind the lines

passages.text: In the dark you go forward with the storming party. No muskets loaded, only bayonets, so no shot gives them away. You climb over sharpened stakes. Men fall beside you, hit in the dark. Colonel Alexander Hamilton leads his men over the wall of one redoubt. The fighting is hand to hand, screaming, steel on steel. You take a cut across the arm but you keep going. The British strongpoints fall. The last walls around Cornwallis are broken.

choices.text: Hold the captured redoubt through the night

passages.text: You stay behind the lines, running powder to the great guns. All night the cannon hammer Yorktown. The ground shakes. You watch the storming parties go forward in the dark and come back fewer. You keep your head down and do your job. You are alive when the sun comes up, and the British outer forts have fallen. The end is close now.

choices.text: Move up to watch the British answer

passages.text: On October 19, 1781, the British march out of Yorktown to surrender. Their drums beat a slow, sad tune. Cornwallis claims to be sick and sends another man to hand over his sword. Thousands of British soldiers lay down their muskets in a long field while the American and French armies watch in silence. You stand in the line, arm bandaged or not, and you understand. This is it. The British army in the south is finished.

choices.text: You fought through it and held on to your fire
You survived it but feel hollow and far away
You drifted through it and just want to go home

passages.text: Yorktown all but ends the war. In 1783 the Treaty of Paris makes it real: the United States is free. You ride north one last time as a man, not a boy. You saw Lexington's dead, the ice of the Delaware, the frozen graves of Valley Forge. You carried the Declaration in your own pack. You stayed when staying could have killed you. You did not become hard or empty. You became someone who finished what he started. Whatever country this becomes, a piece of it is yours, and you carry that home for good.

The war ends, but you do not feel it end. You go home to Boston. The stable is still there. The horses still need feeding. But the cold of Valley Forge never fully left your bones, and the faces of the men you buried come to you at night. You won. The country is free. You survived every battle. Yet something in you was left in those frozen trenches, and it does not come back. You are alive, and you are not whole.

Peace comes in 1783. You walk back to Boston with the crowds. People cheer the new nation. You nod along, but it feels like a story that happened to other men. You kept your head down, traded your boots for bread, did the smallest work you could. You are alive and unharmed, and that is all. You feed the horses again. The great words, all men are created equal, hang in the air around you, but you let them pass by, the way you let everything pass by, and you go on as you were.
